435.title: Out of the depths (Psalm 130)
435.hook: my soul waits more than watchmen for the morning
435.howItsDone: Psalm 130 is one of the seven penitential psalms; Catholics traditionally pray the De profundis for the dead, many churches sing it at evening prayer and funerals, and Lutherans sing Luther's hymn version.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Negev's sudden streams, and your line, sow in tears, reap in joy.

Four in the morning on a city wall. The watchman has been up since midnight. Every shadow in the valley could be an enemy, and it's his job to see it first. He knows morning will come; it always has. But knowing doesn't make the last hour shorter. He watches the sky for the first thin gray line along the hills, the sign that he can finally go home and sleep. Anyone who has worked a night shift, sat up with a sick child, or waited for a phone call knows that hour. Today's psalm lives there.
screen: `FOUR A.M. ON THE WALL.` → `EYES ON THE EAST.` → `THE LONGEST HOUR.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred thirty is short, eight verses, and it begins at the bottom. In the King James Bible: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD." Depths is the word for deep water, the kind you go under. In Latin the psalm is known by its first words, De profundis. Then comes a startling question: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" If God kept a record of every wrong, nobody would be left on their feet. The answer comes straight away: "But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared." Not a God with a ledger. A God with forgiveness, which makes him worth revering. Then the waiting. "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning." He says it twice. And then, in the last two verses, the psalmist turns from himself to his whole people: let Israel hope, for with the Lord there is mercy, and plenteous redemption. Christians have long counted this among the seven penitential psalms, prayers of turning back. Martin Luther made it a hymn. Catholics pray the De profundis for the dead, and it is sung at evening prayer. It's also another song of going up, from the pilgrims' collection. Which means the people who sang it out of the depths were walking uphill as they sang.

segments.voice: Name to yourself one thing you're waiting for, a result, a reconciliation, a morning after a long night, and hold it the way the watchman holds the horizon: not grabbing, not giving up. Let each breath out be one more minute closer to the light. If you pray, say my soul waiteth for the Lord; if you don't, simply wait, hoping, without demanding when.
De profundis. Latin for out of the depths, Psalm one hundred thirty's cry from deep water, and a soul waiting for God more than watchmen wait for morning.
Your line: more than watchmen for morning. The last hour is long, and the light still comes. Day four hundred thirty-five, done.

436.title: A weaned child (Psalm 131)
436.hook: I've calmed and quieted my soul like a weaned child with its mother
436.howItsDone: Christians in contemplative traditions often pray Psalm 131 before silent prayer, and it is sung at evening prayer in many churches and monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, De profundis, out of the depths, and your line, more than watchmen for morning.

Watch a nursing baby on a parent's lap. All need: rooting, fussing, grabbing, turning toward the one thing it wants, crying until it gets it. Nothing wrong with that; that's what babies are for. Now watch an older child on the same lap. Weaned. Not hungry, not asking for anything. Just leaning back against a parent's chest, legs dangling, watching the room. Heavy and calm. There because it's a good place to be, and for no other reason. Same lap, same parent, a completely different way of being held. A psalm only three verses long is about that difference.
screen: `A NURSING BABY: ALL NEED.` → `A WEANED CHILD: JUST LEANING.` → `THE SAME LAP.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred thirty-one is three verses long. Here's the first, in the King James Bible: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me." Haughty means lifted up. Lofty eyes are eyes always looking above their station. And exercise myself means busy myself, chase after. The writer has stopped straining after things too big to grasp. Not because they don't matter, but because they're not his to carry. Then verse two: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child." In the book of Samuel, Hannah keeps her boy at home until he's weaned, and only then brings him to the temple. So a weaned child isn't a newborn. It's a small person who no longer needs the breast, and yet still climbs into its mother's lap. That's the picture of the soul here. Not empty of desire. Quieted. With God, not to get something, just to be there. The writer says he did this himself: I have behaved and quieted myself. It took effort to get still. Then the last verse turns outward again, like Psalm one hundred thirty did: "Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever." It's another song of going up, and the heading gives it to David. Some Christian contemplatives use this little psalm as a picture of prayer that asks for nothing.
screen: `NOT HAUGHTY, NOT LOFTY` · `THINGS TOO HIGH FOR ME` · `WEANED: NOT HUNGRY, STILL HELD` · `I HAVE QUIETED MYSELF` · then, large: `MY SOUL IS EVEN AS A WEANED CHILD.`

segments.voice: Set down every request for now: no list, no fixing, no improving yourself, and if something you want comes to mind, let it go by. Lean back into the chair the way a child leans against a parent, and let your breathing be heavy and slow. If you pray, simply rest in God's presence, wordless, like the child in the lap; if you don't, just rest, asking nothing of the minute.
Hannah. The mother in the book of Samuel who kept her son home until he was weaned, the picture behind this psalm's quiet, grown-up trust.
Your line: quieted, like a child. Still wanting, but leaning back at last. See you tomorrow.

437.title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137)
437.hook: exiles weep and hang up their harps; the psalm even holds their rage honestly
437.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 137 in times of exile, grief and injustice; some churches omit its final verses in public worship, while others pray it whole as an honest lament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah's weaned child, leaning back, and your line, quieted, like a child.

A reggae song built from this psalm, and later a disco version, put it on dance floors. People dance to it at weddings and roller rinks, singing about sitting down by the rivers of Babylon. The words are far older than the beat, and the psalm ends somewhere no party goes. Go back to the days after the fall of Jerusalem. The Babylonian army has burned the city and its temple. Its people have been marched east, to the rivers and canals of Babylon. And their captors, in a cruel joke, ask them to sing.
screen: `A SONG ON THE DANCE FLOOR.` → `JERUSALEM IN FLAMES.` → `SING US A SONG OF ZION.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof." Then the cruelty: "For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion." And the answer is the question at the center of the psalm: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?" They won't perform their grief for the people who caused it. Then a vow: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Cunning means skill. A harpist's right hand. Let me never play again if I forget home. Now the hard part. The last three verses turn to rage. They call down judgment on Edom, which cheered the destruction, and on Babylon, and the very last verse blesses whoever would dash Babylon's little ones against the stones. It is hard to hear. And it's in the Bible. Christians have handled it in different ways. Some churches leave those verses out when the psalm is prayed aloud. Augustine and other early writers read the little ones as small evil thoughts, to be dashed against the rock, which they took to be Christ. Other readers see the psalm as honest rage handed over to God in words, instead of acted out in the world. What the psalm doesn't do is pretend. The Bible keeps the tears, the vow and the fury of people who lost everything.
screen: `HARPS HUNG ON THE WILLOWS` · `SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF ZION` · `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM` · `RAGE KEPT IN THE TEXT, HONESTLY` · then, large: `HOW SHALL WE SING THE LORD'S SONG IN A STRANGE LAND?`

segments.voice: Think of people who are where they never chose to be: refugees in camps, families split across borders, a neighbor who moved here and still cooks food that smells like somewhere else. If you pray, hold them before God, by name or simply as they are; if you don't, hold them in mind with care, and let yourself feel a little of what they've lost.
Mesopotamia. The land of rivers and canals where the exiles sat down, wept, and refused to sing for their captors.

438.title: You knit me together (Psalm 139)
438.hook: you know when I sit and rise; if I take the wings of morning, you are there
438.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 139 as a prayer of being known by God; its last verses, "Search me, O God," are often prayed before confession or at the end of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mesopotamia, harps hung on the willows, and your line, how can we sing here?

On a lot of refrigerators there's a small, grainy, black-and-white picture held up by a magnet. You have to squint. A curve that might be a spine. A blur that might be a hand. The people who put it there can tell you exactly which smudge is the nose. Before anyone has held this child, before anyone knows its laugh, it is already known, already loved. Long before ultrasound, a psalm imagined that same hidden beginning, and claimed that someone was watching it closely.
screen: `A GRAINY PICTURE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `KNOWN BEFORE BEING HELD.` → `KNOWN ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off." Sitting down, getting up, a thought before it's finished. Then the writer tries to imagine getting away. "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Up to heaven: you're there. Down to the grave: you're there. "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me." The wings of the morning: fly as fast as the dawn moves across the sky, all the way to the far edge of the sea. Still held. Then the psalm goes inward, to the womb. The King James says, "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb." The Hebrew verb can mean cover, or weave together, which is why many later translations say knit. Two verses on, the writer says he was "curiously wrought" in secret, a phrase for embroidery, colored thread worked by hand. And in between, the line: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Fearfully here means with awe, the way you'd handle something precious. Then a surprise. Near the end, the psalm turns angry: the writer wants God to slay the wicked. And right after, he stops and turns the searchlight on himself: "Search me, O God, and know my heart." See if there's any wicked way in me. A psalm that starts with being searched ends by asking for it.
screen: `MY DOWNSITTING AND MINE UPRISING` · `THE WINGS OF THE MORNING` · `WOVEN, EMBROIDERED IN SECRET` · `SEARCH ME, O GOD` · then, large: `I AM FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Place your hand flat on your heart, so you can feel it beating; it started before you knew you existed, and somebody, the psalm says, was paying attention even then. Feel the breath lift your hand a little, and let it down. If you pray, say the line slowly, I am fearfully and wonderfully made; if you don't, simply feel how carefully you are put together, and let that be enough.

439.title: Everything praise (Psalm 148)
439.hook: sun, moon, sea monsters, snow, kings and children, praise
439.carry: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar
439.howItsDone: Psalm 148 is a traditional morning praise psalm in many churches, and it is echoed in the Benedicite canticle and in hymns such as "All Creatures of Our God and King."

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life curiously wrought in secret, embroidered in the womb. Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made.

A choir director stands up before the concert and takes the roll. Sopranos? Here. Altos? Here. Tenors, basses? Here. Now keep going. Angels? Sun and moon? Stars? Here. Sea monsters? Here. Fire, hail, snow, fog, the stormy wind? Here. Mountains, fruit trees, cedars, wild animals, cattle, creeping things, birds? Kings, judges, young men and young women, old people and children? All here. That roll call is Psalm one hundred forty-eight. It doesn't ask who believes, who is important, or who can carry a tune. It calls everything into the choir.
screen: `SOPRANOS? ALTOS?` → `SEA MONSTERS? HAIL?` → `EVERYTHING INTO THE CHOIR.`

segments.voice: The psalm has two halves, like a camera tilting from the sky down to the ground. First the heavens: angels, hosts, and, in the King James Bible, "Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light." Then, from verse seven, the earth: "Praise the LORD from the earth, ye dragons, and all deeps." Dragons. The Hebrew is tanninim, great sea creatures, the same word Genesis uses for the great sea monsters of the fifth day. Creatures that frightened the ancient imagination are in the choir. Then the weather: "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word." A storm here isn't chaos. It's doing what it was told. Then mountains and fruit trees, beasts and creeping things, and finally people, every rank mixed together: "Both young men, and maidens; old men, and children." Kings stand in the same row as kids. Why should a rock or a snowflake praise? One old answer: not with words, but by being what it is. A cedar praises by growing like a cedar. The list has echoes. In the Greek Bible, the book of Daniel includes a long song of three young men in a furnace, calling on everything from frost to whales to bless the Lord; Catholics and Orthodox read it as scripture, and Anglicans sing it as the Benedicite. And Francis of Assisi wrote his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God through Brother Sun and Sister Moon. The hymn All Creatures of Our God and King comes from it.
screen: `FROM THE HEAVENS: SUN AND MOON` · `FROM THE EARTH: SEA MONSTERS` · `STORMY WIND FULFILLING HIS WORD` · `KINGS IN THE SAME ROW AS CHILDREN` · then, large: `PRAISE YE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Name ten things in creation, slowly, one breath each: the light in the window, a cloud, a crow, a tree you pass every day, rain, your grandmother's hands, a child somewhere laughing, something huge, something tiny. When you reach ten, sit with the whole crowd of them. If you pray, let each name be a small praise; if not, simply let the list be wonder.

440.title: Let everything that has breath (Psalm 150)
440.hook: trumpet, harp, cymbals, dance: the psalter ends in pure praise
440.carry: your breath goes back as praise
440.howItsDone: Christians sing hallelujah (or alleluia) throughout worship, especially at Easter; many Western churches set it aside during Lent, while Orthodox Christians sing it all year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll call of sea monsters, snow and children, all in one choir. Your line: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar.
screen: `A CEDAR PRAISES BY GROWING LIKE A CEDAR.`

segments.voice: You've probably said today's word without thinking. Shouted in a gospel choir. Sung by a whole hall standing up in the middle of a Christmas concert. Muttered when the bus finally shows up after twenty minutes in the rain. It's one of a handful of words that have traveled, nearly unchanged, from ancient Hebrew into dozens of languages. And it's the word the book of Psalms ends on. After a hundred and forty-nine psalms of tears, rage, waiting and thanks, the last one has no story and no request. Just instruments, dancing and one word.
screen: `A GOSPEL CHOIR.` → `THE BUS FINALLY COMES.` → `THE LAST WORD OF THE PSALMS.`

segments.voice: Hallelujah is two Hebrew words joined. Hallelu means praise, and it's plural, a command to a crowd: all of you, praise. Yah is a short form of God's own name. So: everybody, praise the Lord. The King James Bible usually translates it rather than spelling it out, which is why Psalm one hundred fifty begins and ends with "Praise ye the LORD." In between, an orchestra. "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals." The trumpet is likely the shofar, the ram's horn. The timbrel is a hand drum. And organs isn't a pipe organ: in 1611 the word could mean any instrument, and the Hebrew probably means a pipe or flute. The psalm wants it noisy. Then the last line: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Not everything with a voice, or faith, or talent. Everything with breath. The Hebrew word for breath is neshamah, the same word Genesis uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first human. The breath that was given goes back as praise. In the New Testament the word appears only in Revelation, in Greek as alleluia, sung by a great multitude in heaven. Many Western churches stop saying alleluia during Lent and bring it back with joy at Easter; Orthodox Christians keep singing it all year round.

segments.voice: Notice your breathing; it came in this morning without you asking. Breathe in slowly, and on each out-breath let a word ride out: hallelujah, said softly, if you pray, or thanks, or simply the breath itself as gratitude. In, given; out, given back.

441.title: Five books of prayers
441.hook: the Psalms are in five books, like the Torah, and cover every feeling
441.howItsDone: Many Christians pray through the whole book of Psalms regularly: monasteries traditionally chant all 150 every week, and the Book of Common Prayer sets them out to be read through every month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last psalm, all trumpets and cymbals. Your line: your breath goes back as praise.

Open a Bible near the middle and you may well land in the Psalms: a hundred and fifty of them. For a month this path has walked through them: a tree by the water, a cry of my God, my God, a deer at a dry stream, a sparrow at the altar, a weaned child, exiles by the rivers of Babylon, and yesterday, a crash of cymbals. It can feel like a shuffle playlist: grief, then joy, then fury, then a lullaby. But it isn't a pile. Someone arranged it.
screen: `THE MIDDLE OF THE BIBLE.` → `A MONTH IN THE PSALMS.` → `NOT A PILE, A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The Psalms are divided into five books. Book one runs from Psalm one to forty-one; book two, forty-two to seventy-two; book three, seventy-three to eighty-nine; book four, ninety to one hundred six; book five, one hundred seven to one hundred fifty. You can see the seams. The first four books each end with a blessing, like a door closing, and the fifth ends with yesterday's hallelujah. The first one, in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen." At the end of book two there's a surprising little note: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended." Except they aren't. More psalms of David come later. Some scholars think that line is left over from an older collection, a sign the book was gathered from earlier collections. An old Jewish commentary says that as Moses gave Israel five books of the law, David gave them five books of psalms. Inside, every feeling has a place. Lament runs all through it: complaint, grief, why, how long. Then praise, thanks, pilgrim songs, wisdom, songs for kings. Athanasius, a bishop of Alexandria, wrote that the other books of the Bible speak to you, but the Psalms speak for you; you find your own soul in them, as in a mirror. John Calvin later called the book an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. One more note: Greek and Latin Bibles number most psalms one lower, which is why Catholic and Orthodox prayer books can look off by one.
screen: `FIVE BOOKS, FIVE SEAMS` · `THE PRAYERS OF DAVID ARE ENDED` · `LAMENT RUNS ALL THROUGH IT` · `A MIRROR FOR THE SOUL` · then, large: `EVERY FEELING HAS A PSALM.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly how you are, tired, grateful, angry, waiting, homesick, and let one of this month's psalms rise that fits: the deer at the dry stream, out of the depths, the weaned child, the new song. Pick the one that sounds like you, not the one you think you should, and if you pray, pray it.
Athanasius. The bishop of Alexandria who wrote that the Psalms speak for you, so that you find your own soul in them, as in a mirror.
Your line: every feeling has a psalm. The week ran from the depths to Hannah's weaned child, Babylon, being knit together, everything praising, and hallelujah. That's a whole book, done.
